analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses in employment, consumer, and civil rights contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 81 House cosponsors but never received a committee vote, dying in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to require workers, consumers, and people bringing civil rights claims to give up their day in court before a dispute even happens. Companies use these clauses in job paperwork and product contracts to steer disputes into private arbitration, where proceedings are secret, arbitrators are paid by the company, and appeals are nearly impossible. The bill would let people choose arbitration freely after a dispute arises, but not force it on them in advance, and it would leave business-to-business arbitration untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers who signed contracts containing forced arbitration clauses, including people with discrimination, wage, credit, and product claims, would regain the ability to take those disputes to a public court instead of a private arbitrator chosen under company-drafted terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers in arbitration-bound contracts

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration agreement would be valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, or civil rights dispute, so affected workers and consumers could go to court instead.
The bill preserves voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises; its findings state arbitration can be acceptable when consent is truly voluntary.

A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies and whether an arbitration agreement is valid, removing the common arrangement where the arbitrator rules on the arbitrator's own power.

Arbitration under collective bargaining agreements is exempt, protecting existing union contracts, though union arbitration could not waive an employee's right to enforce statutory and constitutional rights in court.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that embed forced arbitration clauses in employment and consumer contracts, including large employers, financial firms, and other consumer-facing businesses, would lose the shield of private, confidential arbitration and face public court proceedings. Arbitration providers would lose the stream of cases those clauses generate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, consumer businesses, arbitration providers

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to disputes arising after enactment, so people already trapped by signed forced arbitration agreements would get no relief under this bill.

Critics of restricting arbitration note that court litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for small-value claims, so sending every dispute to court could make some claims impractical to bring at all; the bill's own findings concede arbitration can be acceptable when truly voluntary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real: forced arbitration clauses appear in most employment and consumer contracts, and they send claims to confidential proceedings with no meaningful appeal before an arbitrator the company effectively pays for. The honest cost is that court is not always the faster or cheaper forum for small disputes, so the bill trades certainty and speed for transparency and public precedent. The prospective-only effective date means it helps future disputes but not people already bound.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the Arbitration Fairness Act of 2011 on May 12, 2011, with 61 original cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on June 1, 2011, to the Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor during the 112th Congress.
The bill finished with 81 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Senate companion action recorded in the provided materials.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and consumer-facing companies that rely on forced arbitration clauses, and the arbitration industry that supplies them, kept the existing system: workers and consumers remained bound by the clauses the bill would have voided. The full record of this outcome is in the bill's action history [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and arbitration providers kept forced arbitration

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 61 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 81 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none advanced it beyond referral.

against.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill up for a committee markup or vote in the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 81 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor appears in the record; the bill died in committee under Republican control of the House Judiciary Committee.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers (JAMS, AAA and similar firms)
industries.note: Their fee revenue depends on cases generated by predispute arbitration clauses; the bill would eliminate the mandatory stream of employment, consumer, and civil rights cases while leaving business-to-business arbitration intact.

These employers currently channel discrimination, wage, and other workplace claims into confidential arbitration; the bill would open those claims to public court, where rulings create precedent and media scrutiny.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses, banks and credit providers
industries.note: The bill covers consumer disputes involving property, services, money, and credit, so credit card, securities, and consumer contracts could no longer force disputes into arbitration.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers and civil rights attorneys
industries.note: Restoring court access to millions of claims expands the caseload these attorneys can pursue, and their interest runs alongside workers' and consumers' access to court.
